# Federation Between Capability Indexes: Crawl, Reciprocal Identification and Admission

## Abstract

This document describes how independently operated capability indexes discover each other by following discovery documents, how a reading index identifies itself to the index it reads, and an admission model that distinguishes a peer that is known from a peer whose catalogue is indexed. It also describes how an index can preview a peer's catalogue before admitting it. Payment, identity, reputation and invocation are out of scope. The document is intended as input to the DAWN gap analysis on federation between directories.¶

This Internet-Draft is submitted in full conformance with the provisions of BCP 78 and BCP 79.【Each index is an HTTPS server that publishes a discovery document [DISCOVERY]. Indexes find each other by following those documents, a reading index identifies itself to the index it reads, and each index decides per peer whether to index that peer's catalogue. There is no shared infrastructure and no central registration.¶

Catalogue exchange and trust are outside the initial DAWN charter. This document uses DAWN terminology because cooperating indexes that exchange catalogues need these mechanisms, and is offered as input to the gap analysis, not as a proposal for adoption.¶

### 1.1. Scope

This document specifies:¶

  * a crawl protocol over discovery documents (Section 2);¶

  * reciprocal identification of the reading index (Section 3);¶

  * an announcement message (Section 4);¶

  * an admission model (Section 5);¶

  * catalogue preview for peers not yet admitted (Section 5.5).【--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

### [Dawn] Two individual drafts: a marketplace discovery document, and federation between capability indexes

Александр Артамохов <alexar76@rambler.ru> Fri, 30 October 2026 07:11 UTC
Subject: [Dawn] Two individual drafts: a marketplace discovery document, and federation between capability indexes
List-Id: "The list is for discussion of the scope, use cases, requirements, and solutions for discovery of entities (e.g., tasks, AI agents, or endpoints) using IETF technologies." <dawn.ietf.org>
Archived-At: <https://mailarchive.ietf.org/arch/msg/dawn/4NQ7qA-xngkbi3pHhSXu5aomu_Q>
    
    Hello, Two individual drafts that I hope are useful input to DAWN, both written from a federation of capability indexes that has run since mid-2026: draft-artamokhov-dawn-marketplace-discovery-00 (Standards Track) https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-artamokhov-dawn-marketplace-discovery/ https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-artamokhov-dawn-marketplace-discovery/ A discovery document at a well-known URI carrying the public properties a client needs before using a capability index (name, protocol versions, catalogue URI, signing key), the requirements a signed catalogue has to meet, key pinning, and one concrete signature profile with its byte-exact canonicalisation and a strict Ed25519 verification rule. This is the part I believe sits inside the charter: initial discovery of public properties, with integrity. draft-artamokhov-dawn-index-federation-00 (Experimental) https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-artamokhov-dawn-index-federation/ https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-artamokhov-dawn-index-federation/ How independently operated indexes find one another by following discovery documents, identify themselves to the indexes they read, and admit peers without conflating “known to exist” with “indexed”. It is offered against gap 6.2 of draft-jimenez-dawn-discovery-landscape (“no interoperable federation between directories”), knowing that catalogue exchange and trust are outside the first phase; it is input to the gap analysis, not a request for adoption. Both carry an RFC 7942 Implementation Status section that says plainly where this stands: a reference implementation deployed on six public indexes, three further implementations written from the text (same author), two peers run by unrelated operators, and no independent implementation yet. A live discovery document is at https://modelmarket.dev/.well-known/agent-marketplace https://modelmarket.dev/.well-known/agent-marketplace and a conformance runner with signed and negative test vectors is in the repository the drafts cite. If the use-cases draft (draft-kay-dawn-use-cases) has room in its section 8 classes, “cooperating capability indexes exchanging catalogues under existing trust” is the case these two documents come from. Comments on the mailing list are welcome; I will fold them into -01. Aleksandr Artamokhov--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What is MalPkg?

MalPkg is a community-accessible platform that aggregates malicious package indicators, metadata, classifications, and timelines from major software ecosystems. Our mission is to help defenders identify supply-chain risks early and protect their software infrastructure.

### Aggregated Data

Consolidated threat intelligence from multiple package repositories and security research.

### Timely Updates

Near real-time detection and cataloging of newly discovered malicious packages.

### Defensive Focus

Built for security teams to strengthen their supply-chain defenses.

Cross-ecosystem correlation and unified view of malicious packages from PyPI, npm, RubyGems, NuGet, and more.

Behavioral analysis, metadata inspection, and dependency heuristics to identify suspicious patterns.

Export data in JSON, STIX/TAXII formats with full API integration for automated workflows.

### Package Timeline & Diffing

Track version-to-version changes and analyze risk evolution over the package lifecycle.

Advanced queries by ecosystem, author, tags, IOCs, risk scores, and more.

Configure alerts for new threats matching your dependencies or watch criteria.

Supply-chain attacks are among the fastest-growing threats in cybersecurity

MalPkg provides the intelligence needed to stay ahead of these threats, enabling proactive defense rather than reactive incident response.

    Abstract:
    
       Autonomous software agents obtain capabilities from services
       catalogued by independently operated indexes.  For an agent, or
       another index, to use such a catalogue it must first learn a small
       set of public properties of the index: what it is called, which
       protocol versions it speaks, where its catalogue is, and which key
       signs that catalogue.  This document specifies a JSON discovery
       document served at a well-known URI that carries exactly those
       properties, and the requirements a signed catalogue referenced from

       are the subject of a companion document.

# Federation Between Capability Indexes: Crawl, Reciprocal Identification and Admission

This document describes how independently operated capability indexes discover each other by following discovery documents, how a reading index identifies itself to the index it reads, and an admission model that distinguishes a peer that is known from a peer whose catalogue is indexed. It also describes how an index can preview a peer's catalogue before admitting it. Payment, identity, reputation and invocation are out of scope. The document is intended as input to the DAWN gap analysis on federation between directories.¶

## 1. Introduction

Capability indexes are operated by many independent parties, and each lists only what its operator has seen. A client sees only the catalogue of the index it queries, and a provider has to register with each index separately.¶

[I-D.jimenez-dawn-discovery-landscape] (Section 6.2) identifies the lack of an interoperable federation mechanism between directories as a gap. Existing designs federate through a shared distributed hash table [I-D.mp-agntcy-ads], through configured trust relationships [I-D.pioli-agent-discovery], or not at all ([A2A] leaves registries to deployments; [MCPREG] has one upstream registry with mirrors).¶

This document describes a simpler arrangement. Each index is an HTTPS server that publishes a discovery document [DISCOVERY]. Indexes find each other by following those documents, a reading index identifies itself to the index it reads, and each index decides per peer whether to index that peer's catalogue. There is no shared infrastructure and no central registration.¶

Catalogue exchange and trust are outside the initial DAWN charter. This document uses DAWN terminology because cooperating indexes that exchange catalogues need these mechanisms, and is offered as input to the gap analysis, not as a proposal for adoption.¶

### 1.1. Scope

This document specifies:¶

  * a crawl protocol over discovery documents (Section 2);¶

  * reciprocal identification of the reading index (Section 3);¶

  * an announcement message (Section 4);¶

  * an admission model (Section 5);¶

  * catalogue preview for peers not yet admitted (Section 5.5).¶

It does not specify payment, identity of providers or operators, reputation or ranking, invocation, or resolution of conflicting listings.¶

### 1.2. Requirements Language

The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 [RFC2119] [RFC8174] when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.¶

### 1.3. Terminology

Index, catalogue, discovery document, reader:

### I-D Action: draft-artamokhov-dawn-index-federation-00.txt

internet-drafts@ietf.org Fri, 30 October 2026 06:51 UTC
    
    Internet-Draft draft-artamokhov-dawn-index-federation-00.txt is now available.
    
       Title:   Federation Between Capability Indexes: Crawl, Reciprocal Identification and Admission
       Author:  Aleksandr Artamokhov
       Name:    draft-artamokhov-dawn-index-federation-00.txt
       Pages:   15
       Dates:   2026-10-29
    
    Abstract:
    
       Independently operated indexes of invocable capabilities do not
       interoperate: an agent that queries one index cannot see what another
       lists, and a provider must enrol with every index separately.  This
       document specifies how such indexes find one another by following
       discovery documents, how an index identifies itself to the indexes it
       reads so that discovery is not one-directional, and an admission
       model that separates knowing a peer exists from indexing its
       catalogue, so that an open federation does not become an open
       injection point.  It also specifies how an index may preview a peer's
       catalogue before admitting it.  Payment, identity, reputation and
       invocation are out of scope.  The document is offered as input to the
       gap analysis on federation between directories.
